title_en: Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan v. Pearl River Film Production Company and Wang Jin — copyright infringement dispute
keywords_en: Civil; dispute over copyright infringement; second instance; High People's Court; Guangdong Province; natural person; legal person; General Principles of the Civil Law; Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation); whether the director's re-creation constitutes infringement; whether additions and deletions to the original work constitute substantive changes; dismissal of claims; adaptation of film literary script; replacement of director; modification of shooting script; copyright; dispute over copyright infringement between company and Wang Jin
full_text_en:
Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan v. Pearl River Film Studio and Wang Jin

— Dispute over copyright infringement

Plaintiff: Chen Lizhou, male, 34 years old, director of Pearl River Film Studio.

Plaintiff: Wang Yan, female, 31 years old, actress of the Actors Troupe of Pearl River Film Studio.

Agent ad litem: Wang Xiaobin, lawyer of Guangdong Foreign Economic Law Office.

Defendant: Pearl River Film Studio.

Legal representative: Sun Changcheng, General Manager of Pearl River Film Studio.

Agent ad litem: Xu Kang, Deputy Director of the Production Department of Pearl River Film Studio.

Defendant: Wang Jin, male, 47 years old, Deputy General Manager of Pearl River Film Studio.

Agent ad litem: Yu Deshui, Director of the Art Research Office of Pearl River Film Studio.

Agent ad litem: Cai Xiaoying, lawyer of Guangzhou Foreign Economic Law Office.

On September 29, 1987, the plaintiffs Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan filed a lawsuit with the Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court of Fujian Province, alleging that the defendant Wang Jin had infringed the copyright of their film literary script "The Festival of Widow Village". Since the domicile of the defendant sued by the plaintiffs was in Guangzhou, the Quanzhou Intermediate People’s Court of Fujian Province, in accordance with Article 20 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China (for Trial Implementation), transferred the case to the Guangzhou Intermediate People’s Court of Guangdong Province. After accepting the case, the Guangzhou Intermediate People’s Court found that Pearl River Film Studio was a necessary party to the joint action but had not participated in the proceedings, and therefore, in accordance with Article 91 of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation), decided to add it as a defendant. The court formed a collegial panel according to law and, after a public hearing, found the following:

The plaintiffs Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan completed the film literary script "The Festival of Widow Village" and the shooting script in early 1987. In April 1987, Pearl River Film Studio decided to adopt the film literary script for film production, with Chen Lizhou as the director, and paid Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan a manuscript fee of 8,000 yuan as prescribed, thereby obtaining the right to produce the film based on the script. In early August 1987, while the production team was filming in Quanzhou, Fujian Province, a conflict arose between Chen Lizhou and the production staff, making it difficult to proceed with the filming. Pearl River Film Studio decided to replace Chen Lizhou with Wang Jin as the director, while retaining Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan as the screenwriters. After taking over, Wang Jin wrote a film shooting script. This shooting script and the filmed movie "Widow Village" made additions and deletions to the original work "The Festival of Widow Village" in terms of certain plots, characters, time-space, scenes, etc. However, the revised "Widow Village" remained essentially consistent with the original in its theme, main plot, and main character relationships.

The plaintiffs alleged that the defendant’s film shooting script made extensive deletions and changes to many main plots, details, dialogues, and character descriptions of the original work. For example, it completely removed the descriptions of Crow Egg Hill (Crow Egg Hill is a pile of large black rocks by the sea, serving as a place for the activities of the main characters), thereby deviating from the conception and style emphasized in the original work and damaging the unique mood and charm of the original. The defendant had altered the original work, violating Article 118 of the General Principles of the Civil Law of the People’s Republic of China. The plaintiffs requested cessation of the infringement, an apology, and compensation for losses.

The defendants Pearl River Film Studio and Wang Jin argued that the film shooting script written by Wang Jin respected the original film literary script in terms of theme, main plot, and main character relationships. The plaintiffs’ claim that Crow Egg Hill, a pile of rocks, embodied the author’s conception was an imagined inference. They requested the dismissal of the plaintiffs’ claims.

The Guangzhou Intermediate People’s Court held after trial that Wang Jin, as the director of the film "Widow Village", made additions and deletions to certain plots, details, dialogues, environment, scenes, and character actions of the original work "The Festival of Widow Village" in the shooting script he wrote and the filmed movie "Widow Village". The original work had 84 sections, of which 21 sections described Crow Egg Hill and the activities of the main characters on Crow Egg Hill. The film shooting script changed 11 sections related to Crow Egg Hill to “black rocks” and “hillock land”, and deleted the other 10 sections. The description of Crow Egg Hill in the original work was merely a depiction of a localized natural landscape of Widow Village and served only as a partial background for the characters’ activities, playing a supporting role in expressing the theme of the script. With reference to the provisions of the Ministry of Culture’s "Several Provisions on the Work of Film Literature in Feature Film Studios", which state that “after accepting a literary script approved by the studio leadership, the director should carry out the re-creation of the director’s art on the premise of fully respecting the foundation of the literary script (theme, main plot, and main character relationships), so as to realize the intention of the script and improve the quality of the film,” Wang Jin’s actions fell within the permissible scope of the director’s artistic re-creation and did not constitute a substantial change to the descriptions of the theme, main plot, and main character relationships of the plaintiffs’ "The Festival of Widow Village". The plaintiffs’ claim that the defendants altered the original work based on the deletion of descriptions of Crow Egg Hill could not be established. The plaintiffs’ allegation of copyright infringement lacked factual basis and did not comply with Article 118 of the General Principles of the Civil Law. Accordingly, on August 29, 1988, the court rendered a judgment: dismissing the claims of the plaintiffs Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan.

The plaintiffs Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Guangdong High People’s Court, requesting a reversal of the judgment and an order for the defendants Wang Jin and Pearl River Film Studio to apologize and compensate for losses. Pearl River Film Studio and Wang Jin responded, requesting that the original judgment be affirmed.

The Guangdong High People’s Court held after trial that the additions and deletions made by the appellees Wang Jin and Pearl River Film Studio to the original work "The Festival of Widow Village" during the production of the film "Widow Village" did not constitute major changes to the main storyline, main connotation, and main character relationships of the original work. The deletions and changes were within the permissible scope of the director’s re-creation activities. The first-instance judgment was correct, and the appeal grounds of Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan could not be sustained. Upon discussion and decision by the Adjudication Committee of the court, in accordance with Item (1) of Article 151 of the Civil Procedure Law (for Trial Implementation), on December 6, 1989, the court rendered a judgment: dismissing the appeal of the appellants Chen Lizhou and Wang Yan and affirming the original judgment.
